title: Chapter 6 — The Street
paragraphs: If I'd been astonished at first seeing someone as outlandish as Queequeg strolling through the polite society of a civilized town, my surprise quickly vanished during my first daylight walk through New Bedford's streets.

In the streets near the docks, any sizable seaport will often put on view the strangest-looking nondescripts from foreign parts. Even on Broadway and Chestnut Street, Mediterranean sailors will sometimes jostle the frightened ladies. Regent Street is no stranger to Lascars and Malays; and at Bombay, on the Apollo Green, live Yankees have often scared the natives. But New Bedford beats every Water Street and Wapping. In those last-mentioned haunts you see only sailors; but in New Bedford, actual cannibals stand chatting on street corners — savages outright, many of whom still carry unholy flesh on their bones. It makes a stranger stare.

But besides the Fijians, Tongatobooarrs, Erromanggoans, Pannangians, and Brighggians, and besides the wild specimens of the whaling trade who reel unnoticed about the streets, you will see other sights still more curious, and certainly more comical. Every week scores of green Vermonters and New Hampshire men arrive in this town, all thirsting for gain and glory in the fishery. They are mostly young, with stalwart frames — fellows who have felled forests and now want to drop the axe and snatch up the whale-lance. Many are as green as the Green Mountains they came from. In some things you would think them only a few hours old. Look there! That fellow strutting around the corner. He wears a beaver hat and a swallow-tailed coat, belted with a sailor's belt and sheath-knife. Here comes another in a sou'wester and a bombazine cloak.

No town-bred dandy can compare with a country-bred one — I mean a downright bumpkin dandy, a fellow who in the dog-days of summer will mow his two acres in buckskin gloves for fear of tanning his hands. Now when a country dandy like this takes it into his head to make himself a distinguished reputation, and joins the great whale fishery, you should see the comical things he does when he reaches the seaport. Ordering his sea outfit, he has bell-buttons put on his waistcoats and straps on his canvas trousers. Ah, poor Hay-Seed! How bitterly those straps will burst in the first howling gale, when you are driven, straps, buttons, and all, down the throat of the tempest.

But don't think that this famous town has only harpooners, cannibals, and bumpkins to show its visitors. Not at all. Still, New Bedford is a strange place. If it hadn't been for us whalemen, that tract of land might to this day be in as howling a condition as the coast of Labrador. As it is, parts of its back country are enough to frighten you, they look so bony. The town itself is perhaps the most expensive place to live in all New England. It is a land of oil, true enough — but not like Canaan, a land also of corn and wine. The streets do not run with milk; nor in springtime do they pave them with fresh eggs. Yet in spite of this, nowhere in all America will you find more patrician-looking houses, or more opulent parks and gardens, than in New Bedford. Where did they come from? How were they planted on this once scraggy cinder-heap of a country?

Go and gaze at the iron harpoons set as emblems around that lofty mansion over there, and your question will be answered. Yes; all these fine houses and flowery gardens came from the Atlantic, Pacific, and Indian oceans. One and all, they were harpooned and dragged up here from the bottom of the sea. Can Herr Alexander, the stage conjurer, perform a trick like that?

In New Bedford, they say, fathers give whales to their daughters as dowries, and portion off their nieces with a few porpoises apiece. You must go to New Bedford to see a brilliant wedding; for, they say, they have reservoirs of oil in every house, and every night recklessly burn spermaceti candles down to their full length.

In summertime the town is sweet to see, full of fine maples — long avenues of green and gold. And in August, high in the air, the beautiful and bountiful horse-chestnuts, like candelabra, offer the passer-by their tapering upright cones of clustered blossoms. So all-powerful is art, which in many a district of New Bedford has laid bright terraces of flowers over the barren refuse rocks thrown aside on creation's final day.

And the women of New Bedford bloom like their own red roses. But roses bloom only in summer; the fine carnation of their cheeks is perennial as sunlight in the seventh heaven. Nowhere else can you match that bloom — except in Salem, where they say the young girls breathe such musk that their sailor sweethearts can smell them miles offshore, as if they were approaching the fragrant Moluccas instead of the Puritan sands.
